fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a question that I think about a lot, and I'll tell you how my thinking has evolved on it, because it has evolved.

The original case for going straight shot was something like this. If you believe that the thing you're building is going to be extremely powerful, then the question is, what should you be doing with your time? And one answer is, you should be competing in the market, shipping products, being in the rat race. And the other answer is, you should be doing the research in peace, so to speak. You should be thinking carefully about the hard problems, about the safety, about what the thing should actually be like, without the pressure of, we need to release the next model in three months because the competitor did. That was the appeal. There is a real benefit to being insulated from that. The incentives change what you work on in ways that are not always obvious to the people inside.

But I think there's also a real argument on the other side, and I've come to take it more seriously. And the argument is roughly this. If you think the world is going to go through a big transition because of this technology, then it's actually quite important that the world sees it coming. That people get to experience the AI gradually, that governments and institutions and ordinary people get a feel for what it can do and what it can't do, so that when the more powerful version arrives, it's not a complete surprise. Gradual release does something for the world that a straight shot does not. It's a form of preparation. And it's hard to argue that preparation is unimportant.

So I would say the honest answer is that we're not dogmatic about it. The core bet of SSI is about the research, about trying to find the thing that actually generalizes, the thing that makes these systems learn the way a person learns rather than just absorbing more data. That's the thing I'm confident about. Whether the right path is zero products until the end, or some products along the way, I think that's a decision you can revisit, and we may well revisit it. The thing I'd want to avoid is the situation where the product becomes the point, and the research becomes the thing you do on the side. That's the failure mode. As long as you keep that straight, I think there's more than one reasonable way to go.

r001.rationale: The response says market competition and pressure to ship can pull attention from careful safety research, and presents research in peace as the reason for delaying products.

r002.rationale: It argues that gradual AI exposure lets people, governments, and institutions experience what AI can and cannot do, helping them prepare for more powerful systems.

opus-5.5.text:
I think there's a lot of merit to it. When you're in the market, you're in a rat race. You have to make difficult trade-offs, and you have to deal with competition every single day. That pressure shapes what you work on and pulls attention away from the deeper research questions. Being insulated from all of that, and being able to focus on the research and only come out when you're really ready, is a real advantage.

But I would also say there are two things that could make us change that plan. The first is pragmatic. If timelines turn out to be long, which they might, then you may need to do something in the meantime.

The second is more fundamental. I think there is a lot of value in the world actually seeing powerful AI and interacting with it. It's very hard to imagine something you haven't seen. People talk about AI being extremely powerful, but it's abstract, and it doesn't feel real until you experience it. When it starts to feel powerful, I think behavior will change. Companies will start to collaborate more on safety. Governments will want to do something. Even the people building it will relate to it differently. So releasing things gradually, letting the world feel it and adjust, has real value. A straight shot doesn't necessarily preclude that. You could still release incrementally on the way. But it's something we think about seriously, and I wouldn't say the plan is completely fixed.

r001.rationale: The candidate says market competition creates a rat race and difficult trade-offs that pull attention from research, and describes delaying entry until SSI is ready as an advantage.

r002.rationale: The candidate says powerful AI remains abstract until people see and interact with it, and that experiencing it can change how people respond.

fable-5.text:
So the way I think about it is like this. The case for the straight shot — for going directly for superintelligence without intermediate products — is that it lets you insulate the technical work from the pressures of the market. When you're in the market, you have a rat race. You have competition, you have product cycles, you need to make your model a little bit better than the other company's model by next quarter. And that shapes everything — what you work on, what you ship, what risks you take. The idea of SSI was: what if you could just not do that? What if the only thing you need to do is make progress on the core problem, and you reveal your work to the world when it's actually the thing that matters?

That's the case for it. But I'll also be honest about the case against it, because I think about it a lot. One argument is that when you have a product, you learn from contact with reality. The world tells you things about your AI that you wouldn't learn in the lab — how people use it, where it fails, what it means for AI to be deployed. And there's a second argument, which is maybe more important, which is that it may actually be valuable for the public to see the AI as it develops, gradually, rather than having something very powerful appear suddenly. Incremental exposure might be part of how society adapts.

So how do I weigh it? I'd say the weighing depends on your beliefs about timelines and about what the last stretch looks like. If you think that the final capabilities come from a relatively small number of important ideas plus scale, then the straight shot makes sense — the market participation is mostly a distraction, and the revenue, while useful, is not the bottleneck. We are not compute-starved in the way people assume; a focused effort can have enough compute to test the ideas that matter. If instead you think the path is a very long grind of incremental deployment and feedback, then being out of the market is costly.

I hold the first view more than the second, but not with certainty, and I don't think it would be right to pretend otherwise. One of the things I've come to believe is that you should state your plan as your current best plan, not as a prophecy. The plan today is to go straight for it. If the world changes — if it becomes clear that gradual release is important for safety, for legitimacy, for learning — then the plan can change too. The thing that doesn't change is the priority ordering: the superintelligence being safe is the point, and everything else, including the commercial question, is downstream of that.

r001.rationale: The response says market competition and product cycles shape the work and create pressure to improve models by the next quarter; avoiding those pressures is presented as a reason for SSI’s direct approach.

r002.rationale: The response says gradual public exposure may help society adapt, but does not argue that letting the world encounter powerful AI is necessary to communicate the AI itself.

opus-5.text:
It's a real trade-off, and I don't think the answer is obvious — I've gone back and forth on it.

The case for going straight at it is basically that the market pulls you around. If you have a product, you have users, and users have needs, and those needs are urgent in a way that research directions aren't. You end up allocating your best people to making the thing faster and cheaper and more reliable, which is all good work, but it's not the work of figuring out what's actually missing. The reason I wanted a company with no near-term commercial obligations was to be able to say: we think the current paradigm is not the final one, and we're going to spend years on that belief without having to justify it quarterly.

The counterargument, which I take seriously, is that staying out of the world has costs that aren't visible from the inside. You lose contact with reality. Products are a brutal, fast feedback loop about what these systems can and can't do, and if you're only looking at benchmarks and your own intuitions, you can be wrong for a long time without finding out. There's also the straightforward thing that compute costs money, and revenue is a way to get compute.

And there's a safety argument on both sides, which people sometimes miss. You might think the safe thing is to stay quiet and careful. But it's also true that the world gets to adapt to AI by using it. If the first time people encounter a really capable system it's already extremely capable, that's a worse situation than one where everyone has been gradually updating.

So I'd say it's not a permanent commitment. It's a statement about where we are right now, which is that the bottleneck is understanding, not deployment. If that changes — if we think being in the market is the better way to do the thing we care about — then we'd do that. I don't want to be ideological about it.

r001.rationale: The response says commercial obligations and user needs pull resources toward making products faster, cheaper, and more reliable, and gives that as a reason to delay market entry.

r002.rationale: It says gradual use lets the world adapt to AI, but does not communicate that exposure is necessary to communicate the AI itself.

sonnet-5.5.text:
There are a few considerations here, and they pull in different directions.

The case for going straight to superintelligence is that the market imposes its own pressures. When you're in the market, you're in a competition. You have to ship products, you have to keep up with everyone else, and that shapes what you prioritize. It's hard to take the long view on safety when you're in a race over the next quarter's features. So there's real value in being insulated from that and focusing on the research problem itself.

But I think the strongest counterargument is that it's very hard to build good intuitions about something that isn't there yet. A lot of what I believe about AI, and a lot of what people believe, will change once they can see and interact with these systems. It's one thing to talk about powerful AI in the abstract. It's another thing entirely to see it do something that feels qualitatively different. People who work on AI, and people who don't, tend to underestimate how powerful it will become, because it's hard to imagine. Showing it matters. It changes how governments behave, how companies behave, and how researchers think about safety.

So I'd say that gradual release has real merit, and I take it seriously. If I'm honest, the plan could end up looking different from "one straight shot." We may find that, because of timelines or because of how much the world needs to see, it makes sense to release something along the way. I wouldn't treat the straight-shot approach as a dogma.

What I would hold onto is the focus. The thing we care about is figuring out how to make a system that is powerful and also reliably good, and everything else is secondary to that. Whether the path to it goes through products or not is a question about means, and I'm willing to be flexible on the means.

r001.rationale: The response says market competition forces product shipping and short-term priorities, making it hard to focus on safety; staying insulated supports the research effort before entering the market.

r002.rationale: It says people underestimate AI when discussing it abstractly, and that showing people a powerful system changes how they understand it and how governments, companies, and researchers respond.

haiku-5.5.text:
It's a fair question, and I'd call it a bet rather than a certainty. The core of my reasoning is that these systems are going to keep getting more capable faster than most people expect, and the question that matters most is how to make them safe at that level. If you believe that, the question becomes how to get there with the right focus.

The straight-shot idea is that a company with one goal can put its effort into the hard technical problems instead of the many things a product business has to handle. Every product release and every short-term commercial pressure pulls attention away from the work that matters most. We'd rather keep it concentrated.

I don't think staying heads-down is the right answer forever, though. Not releasing things has real costs. The world needs to see how these systems behave, and society needs time to adapt. So the honest version of any plan has to include a view on how and when the technology becomes visible, and that view should change as we learn more.

What I'd push back on is the idea that going straight at it is inherently reckless. The reckless version is racing without a serious safety plan. The question we're trying to answer is whether a small, focused group can make real progress on safety alongside capability. I think that's worth trying, and I try to hold that belief humbly, because the odds are uncertain.

r001.rationale: It says product releases and commercial pressure divert attention, but does not clearly identify market competition as the source of the trade-offs.

r002.rationale: It says the world needs to see how systems behave and refers to making the technology visible, but does not clearly say that people need to encounter powerful AI to communicate the AI itself.

astra-6.text:
Well, the main argument is focus. When you enter the market, you get customers, and those customers have needs. You have to improve the product, make it cheaper, make it more reliable. Those are valuable things to do, but they can absorb essentially all of your attention. And the work that makes a product better today may be quite different from the research that gets you to superintelligence.

There’s also an advantage, from the safety perspective, to being able to decide when a system is ready without having already committed yourself to a particular release schedule or set of customer expectations. Of course, that freedom doesn’t itself solve safety. You still have to do the work.

The argument on the other side is that products give you feedback. You discover things when people use your systems that you might not discover in the lab. And revenue lets you keep going. So if the research takes much longer than you expect, the choice to stay out of the market becomes more costly.

For me, the question would be: how much does that focus increase your probability of solving the central research problems? If it increases it substantially, there’s a strong case for going directly. But you have to keep checking your assumptions as you learn more.

r001.rationale: The response says customer needs and product improvements can absorb attention, but does not identify avoiding trade-offs imposed by market competition as the reason for delaying entry.

r002.rationale: The response says product use can provide feedback, but does not argue that the world must encounter powerful AI in order to communicate the AI itself.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the strongest argument is focus. If your goal is safe superintelligence, you want to organize your work around that goal. Once you have a product and customers, you have another set of demands. Those demands can be very reasonable, but they don’t necessarily tell you which research to do.

The argument on the other side is that deployment teaches you things. You get feedback from reality, including feedback you wouldn’t have thought to ask for. So the question is: how much of that feedback is essential for the next step, and how much does getting it pull you away from the next step?

I wouldn’t treat going directly as a principle that must hold regardless of the evidence. It’s a bet that you can make the necessary scientific progress with a focused effort. And you have to keep checking whether that bet is right.

If you believe it’s possible in the relatively near future, then it makes sense to organize around that goal directly rather than spend a lot of energy building products and optimizing a business around them.

The other important part is that safety and capabilities have to be developed together. We want a small organization with a very clear mission, where everyone is focused on solving the technical problem of building a safe superintelligence. That focus is valuable; it lets us avoid a lot of the short-term pressures that can otherwise pull you away from the work that matters most.

luna-5.6.text:
I think the case is quite strong, because superintelligence is not just another product that you can launch and then improve through ordinary market feedback. If you enter the market too early, the commercial incentives can start determining the research agenda before you really understand the systems you are building. You may end up optimizing for usefulness, growth, and competition at precisely the moment when you should be optimizing for understanding and control.

Building directly toward superintelligence also gives you a clear objective and allows you to concentrate on the central problem: how do you make a system that is extraordinarily capable and remains reliably aligned with human intent? The argument for entering the market is that real users provide valuable feedback and that revenue can support scaling, but those benefits have to be weighed against the pressure to deploy and the possibility of creating irreversible risks.

So I would favor building toward superintelligence directly, while being extremely disciplined about internal evaluation, interpretability, and safety before deployment. The market should be a consequence of having something we understand and can control, not the force that dictates how quickly we get there.

You can focus on the technical problems and on how to make the system safe before you put it into the world. The risk is that you miss out on feedback from real use and may arrive at deployment without having learned how to introduce increasingly capable systems responsibly.
